title: Precision Selenium Biofortification of Leafy Vegetables in Controlled-Environment Agriculture: Mechanisms, Production Strategies, Safety, and Research Priorities
content: Selenium (Se) is an essential micronutrient whose dietary supply varies widely because Se concentrations in plant foods depend on geography, substrate chemistry, crop species, and production practices. Agronomic biofortification can raise Se concentrations in edible tissues, but open-field outcomes are often inconsistent because fertilizer fate and plant uptake are governed by soil properties and weather. Controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) allows Se form, concentration, exposure duration, nutrient interactions, and aerial conditions to be regulated more precisely. This review examines the physiological basis of Se uptake and assimilation, the suitability of CEA platforms for Se delivery, the influence of nutrient-solution and environmental factors, effects on yield and phytochemical quality, food-safety considerations, and priorities for commercial deployment. In hydroponic studies, selenate supplied at roughly 2–16 µM typically raised leaf Se by one to two orders of magnitude with little or no yield penalty, whereas higher concentrations reduced biomass in some cultivars. Responses differ among species, cultivars, Se forms, and experimental systems, so universal application rates cannot yet be recommended. We propose that CEA biofortification be designed around a serving-based target window, and that future work prioritize harmonized fresh- and dry-weight reporting, Se speciation, solution mass balance, batch variability, economic evaluation, and commercial-scale validation.
